summary:
TARPU helps small farmers in Arequipa, Peru, understand their own field with NASA data. The farmer outlines a plot on a satellite map and TARPU describes it: elevation and slope (NASADEM), daily climate (NASA POWER), vegetation greenness, surface temperature, evapotranspiration and land cover (MODIS), plus soil properties (ISRIC SoilGrids) and the crops most sown in that altitude zone (Peru's 2012 agricultural census). HLS 30 m and SMAP soil-moisture series are already extracted and are the next layers to connect.
Series are stored by satellite cell, so neighbouring plots reuse data instead of downloading it twice. Every number shows its source, period, scale and missing dates; a missing value is never shown as zero.
A rule engine compares the farmer's crop options with cited FAO EcoCrop ranges, criterion by criterion, with no invented scores. An assistant, by text or voice, explains the results using only TARPU's own evidence. TARPU describes the past: it does not forecast or diagnose frost, stress or soil fertility.
It addresses the challenge by turning scattered NASA datasets into one traceable, plot-level view that a farmer can read, question and download.
details:
TARPU is a decision-support web platform that helps farmers in Arequipa, Peru understand their own fields with open NASA Earth observation data and compare crop options using cited rules. It supports the farmer's judgment and local knowledge; it does not replace them. The interface is in Spanish, for local users.

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

The farmer finds their field on a high-resolution satellite map that also shows three altitude zones (coast, valley, highland) derived from NASADEM, and outlines the field corner by corner. TARPU instantly reads a pre-built regional base for all of Arequipa and shows, for that outline: area; elevation and slope from the 30 m NASADEM pixels inside the field; soil properties from SoilGrids 2.0; the altitude zone and the crops with the largest sown area there (Peru's 2012 Agricultural Census); and NASA POWER daily climate. "Extract complete data" starts a background job that retrieves MODIS series (NDVI, land surface temperature, evapotranspiration, land cover); the app shows the status of each source and lets the user stop the job. A history view summarizes the climate by year. A rotation view takes the declared crop, water source and months and runs a rule engine that compares POWER climate and SoilGrids pH with FAO EcoCrop ranges, criterion by criterion, for four catalog crops, with no scores or weights. A technical study view and a reports view give a printable summary and a JSON download. A guided tour and an assistant (text or voice) explain each section.

Technically, a Python/FastAPI backend uses a "mixed scheme". Static or coarse data is extracted once for the whole region and read in under a second. Heavy satellite series are extracted per coordinate by a worker that takes jobs from a queue in Supabase (Postgres, PostGIS, Storage). Series are stored per satellite cell or pixel, so a neighbouring field in the same pixel reuses them instead of downloading them again. The assistant first builds an answer from TARPU's own evidence; if an AI provider is configured on the server, the model may only rephrase that evidence, and its answer is rejected if it contains a number that is not in the source data.

BENEFITS

Farmers see real NASA and partner data about their own field, in plain language, with its source, period, scale and missing dates. Nothing is hidden behind a score. Reuse by cell lowers the cost of serving many nearby fields. Every file (original, normalized, with provenance) can be downloaded, so results can be checked.

INTENDED IMPACT

To lower the barrier to using Earth observation data in small Andean farming, where fields are small, altitude changes conditions quickly and technical support is scarce. In the long run, TARPU aims to help farmers and local advisers discuss crop and rotation options with evidence they can trace. We have not yet validated it with farmers; the next step is a pilot in the three altitude sectors.

TOOLS

Python 3.13, FastAPI, Pydantic, Shapely, pyproj; Supabase (Postgres + PostGIS + Storage) in Docker; React, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet and TanStack Query; NASA POWER, MODIS (via ORNL DAAC), NASADEM, HLS and SMAP (via AppEEARS); ISRIC SoilGrids, FAO GAEZ and EcoCrop, INEI census data. No special hardware: it runs on an ordinary laptop with Docker, and voice uses the browser's speech recognition and synthesis.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

Every value carries what it means and what it does not: a POWER value describes a cell of about 55 x 67 km, and NDVI is greenness, not fertility. A missing value is never shown as zero, and when there is no cited rule TARPU abstains instead of inventing one. The AI assistant is bounded by evidence: it cannot add numbers. Data is organized by satellite cell, not by field, which is what makes reuse possible.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

The scale mismatch between satellite pixels and small fields; very different conditions by altitude; data quality flags and gaps; honest limits (no forecasts, no diagnosis of frost, stress or soil fertility); older and less technical users (large controls, guided tour, voice); and API keys kept on the server, never in the browser.

STATUS AND LIMITS

It runs locally; its repository reports 14 frontend tests and 37 backend tests passing. Not implemented yet: public deployment and real user accounts (the demo sign-in is local to the browser); HLS and SMAP layers in the app (data already extracted); a validated call to a real AI provider; and cited benefits for rotations.

USE OF AI

Code, data tooling and documentation were written with assistance from Claude (Claude Code) and OpenAI Codex; every use is logged, with author and tool, in entrega/uso-de-ia.md in the repository. The in-app assistant is optional: it only calls an external language model if a key is configured on the server, and the model may only rephrase TARPU's own evidence.
